items.title: The Published Voice: Whose Voice Are We Really Reading?
items.excerpt: Drawing on an EASE panel called 'Beyond Track Changes,' Roohi Ghosh asks what is left of an author's voice once AI-driven editing smooths every manuscript toward the same 'native' register. The piece treats voice as a craft asset that automated editing quietly erodes, and argues editors have to measure their impact on it rather than assume it survives.

items.title: "Avoiding AI" Library Programs, and More Updates For Library Workers
items.excerpt: Public libraries are now running patron workshops on how to opt out of AI — search, assistants, and the defaults baked into everyday software. Book Riot's library-worker roundup treats 'avoiding AI' as a teachable literacy skill, a counter-programming move against the assumption that every reading and research tool should be model-mediated.

items.title: These new features are coming to the iFlytek AINOTE 2
items.excerpt: iFlytek published a 2026 roadmap for its LLM-powered E-Ink tablet, layering AI meeting transcription, automated note organization and document processing on top of a reworked handwriting and PDF toolbar. It is a concrete look at what an AI-native reading-and-writing device wants to become once the model sits underneath the page.

items.title: Princeton University Press Partners with Cashmere on AI Licensing
items.excerpt: Princeton University Press will make its catalogue available to 'copyright compliant' AI platforms through Cashmere, a licensing intermediary built for retrieval-augmented generation rather than model training. The press keeps title-by-title control over what is licensed and on what terms — an early template for how books get into AI answers without being swallowed into weights.

items.title: AI May Be Making Publishing Easier, But It's Still Not Easy
items.excerpt: At the Media Transformation Summit, publishers reported that AI has genuinely lowered production cost — audiobooks especially — while leaving the hard parts untouched: deciding what to publish and finding readers. The recurring practical lesson was that machine-readable metadata and management buy-in, not the model itself, decide whether an AI workflow lands.
